title: Three places on the mountain
about: Dante, a living man, climbs the mountain of Purgatory with the dead poet Virgil as his guide. On the stair above the terrace of envy he asks how a good can make its owners richer the more of them share it. A terrace later, at nightfall, when no one may climb, Virgil explains how the mountain is ordered. At the top Virgil tells him that his will is now free, upright and whole, and Dante walks into the garden of Eden and sees a lady across a stream.

view.says: Auden went back to Virgil’s speech in canto 17 more than once. In 1941 he copied nine lines of it into the notes of *New Year Letter* and quoted their conclusion in a review. In *The Dyer’s Hand* he set three of those lines against *The Tempest*, which in his reading blames nature and makes spirit innocent. Dante, he wrote, holds the exact opposite: what is natural cannot err, and only the mind’s love can.
view.quote: The natural can never desire too much or too little because the natural good is the mean
view.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 130–31; *New Year Letter* (London: Faber, 1941), the note just before the note to line 1432
view.checked: The Dyer's Hand read in the scan, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 6266-6306, and read again by the examiner on 2026-10-03: the passage runs from the foot of p. 130 to p. 131, and the sentence quoted is on p. 131, exact. The note in New Year Letter was seen by the examiner in search snippets of the Faber edition at archive.org (newyearletter0000aude): it quotes canto 17, lines 91-96, a gap, then 103-105 in Okey's wording, is signed with the canto, and stands just before the note headed Line 1432. Not seen in full; its page number was not seen.

lenses.label: Simile
lenses.name: simile
lenses.plain: a comparison that says one thing is like another
lenses.caption: Dante has asked how a good can make its owners richer the more of them share it. Virgil answers with a comparison, marked by così (so) and com’ (as): the good above runs to love as a ray comes to a lucido corpo, a bright body. Lucido is said of a polished surface that throws light back. Landino, commenting in 1481, gives the point: a ray is not made less by the number of bodies it lights. Virgil’s reasoning ends on a second comparison, come specchio, like a mirror: each gives back to the other. Auden copied these last three lines into the notes of New Year Letter in 1941.
lenses.why: A question about dividing goods is answered by likening the good to light and the souls to bright bodies that give it back: light is not made less by the number receiving it. Auden copied the closing lines in 1941.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Dante’s question and Virgil’s words on earthly goods, earlier in [Canto 15](#/read/dante-italian/pur-15:16). Simile as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. *Lucido* in the Treccani *Vocabolario* and the *Enciclopedia Dantesca*. Cristoforo Landino’s commentary of 1481 on these lines, at the Dartmouth Dante Project. Auden: *New Year Letter* (1941), the note to line 1705.

spans.label: what rises: so much it gives

lenses.caption: After the comparison come three statements, and each is a proportion. Tanto and quanto: it gives as much as it finds. Quantunque: however far love reaches, the worth grows on it. Quanta, with più three times: the more souls, the more to love and the more love. A sentence of this build ties two amounts together, so that as one rises the other does. Dante’s question took sharing for division: more owners, so a smaller share, which is what Virgil has just said of earthly goods (lines 49 to 51). Più, more, comes ten times between lines 55 and 75, three of them in the last three lines.
lenses.why: Dante asked a question in division; each statement of the answer is built as a proportion whose two sides rise together, so the grammar states a good that grows with the number who share it.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. *Quanto* and *quantunque* in the Treccani *Vocabolario*. Anna Maria Chiavacci Leonardi’s commentary, which calls lines 70 to 72 a proportion. Dante’s question and Virgil’s words on earthly goods, earlier in [Canto 15](#/read/dante-italian/pur-15:16). A count of *più* in lines 55 to 75 of the Italian printed here; Robert Hollander’s commentary notes the same run of the word.

lenses.caption: Dante’s question is in the words of property: distributo, shared out, posseditor, owners, ricchi, rich (lines 61 to 63). The answer has no word of owning. Its words are of light and love, and two verbs are of giving: the good si dà, gives itself, and each soul rende, gives back. Rendere is first to return what is owed, and is also said of a mirror that sends back an image. Auden quoted the last three lines in an essay on The Merchant of Venice, to show that love breeds love, and went on to usury, where money breeds money.
lenses.why: A question asked in the words of owning is answered in words of light, love and giving back; Virgil has told Dante that his mind is fixed on earthly things. Auden set the lines beside usury, where money breeds money.
lenses.stands: The lines themselves, with Dante’s question and Virgil’s rebuke just before them in [Canto 15](#/read/dante-italian/pur-15:20). Anna Maria Chiavacci Leonardi’s commentary, on the words of light and love. *Rendere* and *valore* in the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* and the Treccani *Vocabolario*, which cite these lines. *Caritas* in Lewis and Short. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 230.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: Okey takes the verb to mean understanding one another. The Italian Dante encyclopedia gives it here an old sense borrowed from Provençal: to love. Longfellow writes *aspire*.
The plain sense is kept: to give back. Longfellow has *reflects*.
*Valore* is worth or power, and here a name for God. Okey writes *goodness*. Longfellow keeps the English word from the same Latin root, *valour*, which now means courage and once meant worth.
*Bright* for *lucido*. Longfellow keeps the look-alike word, *lucid*.

lenses.caption: The English beside the Italian is Okey’s prose, the version Auden set his class to learn and the wording he copied into his notes. It follows Dante closely: bright body, giveth back. At one word the translators part. S’intende becomes comprehend each other, and when Auden quotes the last three lines he brings them in to show that both love and understanding breed their like. Longfellow’s translation has aspire. The Italian Dante encyclopedia and the commentators Sapegno and Chiavacci Leonardi read the verb here in an old sense taken from Provençal, to love. On that reading lines 73 and 74, the seventh and eighth here, hold three verbs for loving and none for knowing.
lenses.why: The prose Auden quotes turns one old verb into comprehend each other, and his remark that love and understanding breed their like matches that wording; the reference work on Dante’s words reads the verb as love.
lenses.stands: The two versions as they stand side by side. Auden’s class and this prose: Donald Pearce’s memoir, p. 153. Auden’s use of the lines: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 230. *Intendere* in the *Enciclopedia Dantesca*, and the commentaries of Natalino Sapegno and Anna Maria Chiavacci Leonardi on line 73. *Valour* in the *Century Dictionary* and *A New English Dictionary*. Longfellow’s words are in [his Canto 15](#/read/dante-longfellow/pur-15:22).

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.caption: Two lines set two loves against each other, turning on ma, but. The first is the love a creature has by nature, and gets è sempre, is always. The second, the love of the mind, gets another verb: puote, can. The same root stands on both sides, errore and errar, first denied and then allowed. In the next canto Virgil explains: the first desire is in man as the urge to make honey is in the bee and earns no praise or blame, and merit begins with the power that keeps the threshold of assent, free will. Auden’s comment: what is natural obeys necessity and cannot picture what might be.
lenses.why: Is always goes with the love a creature cannot help and can with the love of the mind, so one changed verb carries Auden’s point about these lines: nature cannot err, and the blame lies with spirit, which is free.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Antithesis as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Virgil’s own explanation in the next canto, [Canto 18](#/read/dante-italian/pur-18:18): the bee, praise and blame, the threshold of assent, free will. The commentaries of Natalino Sapegno and of Umberto Bosco and Giovanni Reggio, on the two loves. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 130–31.

grounds.claim: the two subjects, the two verbs and the repeated root

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Dante’s rhyme is a chain. In each group of three lines, a tercet, the middle line gives its rhyme to the outer lines of the next. Here the middle line of the first tercet ends on amore, love. The second tercet has to answer it, and answers with errore, error, and vigore, the force that love can have too much or too little of. So the lines about error are rhymed on love. The conclusion states the tie outright: love is the seed of every virtue and of every act that deserves punishment.
lenses.why: The form makes each tercet take its rhyme from the middle line of the one before; Dante ends that line on amore, so the lines on error are rhymed on love, the tie that Virgil’s conclusion states in plain words.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. *Terzina* in the Treccani *Vocabolario*: the middle line of each group of three gives its rhyme to the first and third lines of the next. The conclusion is in the lines themselves.

grounds.claim: which line ends rhyme, and the letters that carry the rhyme

notes.source: Treccani, Vocabolario, sementa; Lewis and Short, sementis

notes.note: Latin *poena* is first a payment that makes good a wrong, then punishment, then pain. On the sixth terrace a soul says he ought to call his *pena* solace (canto 23, line 72).

lenses.caption: Errore and errar come from the Latin for wandering and going astray; being wrong is the second sense. The poem opens with the straight way lost (Inferno 1, line 3). In the lines left out love moves: it si torce, twists, toward evil, or corre, runs, at the good with too much or too little care. In the conclusion love is sementa, seed, of every virtue and of every act that earns pene, penalties or pains. Auden quoted these words near the end of a review of 1941. The love in them, he wrote, is the basic will of every creature to become itself, and grace changes that love and does not add another.
lenses.why: Going wrong is named with a word for straying and love with a word for seed, so good and bad acts are given one origin; Auden read that seed as the love that grace changes and does not destroy.
lenses.stands: *Error*, *erro*, *animus*, *sementis* and *poena* in Lewis and Short. *Errore*, *errare* and *obietto* in the *Enciclopedia Dantesca*; *sementa* in the Treccani *Vocabolario*, which cites this line. The lines left out, in [Canto 17](#/read/dante-italian/pur-17:33), and the opening of [the *Inferno*](#/read/dante-italian/inf-01:0). Auden: “Eros and Agape” (1941), in his *Prose*, vol. II, pp. 137–40.

facts.wordOrder: The Italian line shown names too much before too little; on the mountain too little (terrace 4) lies below too much (terraces 5 to 7). Okey’s prose beside it has too little first, and so does the Italian printed opposite his prose in the Temple Classics edition. The Italian Auden prints in The Dyer’s Hand has that order too.
facts.night: No one can climb the mountain after sunset (7.43-60). The travelers reach the top of the stair as the stars come out (17.70-78), and Dante asks Virgil to go on speaking while their feet are stopped (17.84).
facts.hell: Virgil gives the plan of lower Hell in the same way, during a halt, in Inferno 11.10-24: every malice has injury for its end, done through force or through fraud. Lust is punished in the second circle of Hell, the first after Limbo (Inferno 5.1-2 and 37-39), and is the last sin purged on the mountain (cantos 25 to 27).
facts.auden: Auden on the structure: Forewords and Afterwords (1973), p. 269.
facts.source: every canto and line number was read in the hosted Italian text

lenses.caption: The three ways of going wrong that Virgil names are the plan of the mountain. Love of an evil object is wept for on the three terraces already climbed: pride, envy, anger. Love with too little force is made good on this one. Love with too much is wept for on the three above. Virgil’s plan of lower Hell in Inferno 11 sorts by injury done, through force or fraud; this one sorts by love. The speech comes at night, when no one may climb, and by count of lines the middle of the whole poem falls inside it. Cantos 14 to 20 match in length, pair by pair. Auden noted that Dante’s structure settles even the number of verses.
lenses.why: Given in a halt at the midpoint, after three terraces have been walked, the three errors sort seven sins into one scheme of love with a wrong object or a wrong measure; Auden noted how exactly Dante’s structure is counted.
lenses.stands: Virgil’s speech to the end of [Canto 17](#/read/dante-italian/pur-17:35); the rule of the night in [Canto 7](#/read/dante-italian/pur-07:14); the plan of Hell in [*Inferno* 11](#/read/dante-italian/inf-11:7). The commentaries of Natalino Sapegno and Charles S. Singleton, on which terraces answer to which error. A count of the lines of the Italian printed here; Robert Hollander’s commentary puts the middle of the poem at the same place. Auden: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 269.

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.caption: The verb comes first: m’apparve, there appeared to me. Its subject is kept back through the rest of that line and two more, and until then the sentence does not say what appeared. The wait is filled with a comparison: as a thing appears, suddenly, that through wonder turns every other thought aside. Only then comes una donna soletta, a lady all alone. The poem names her once, five cantos later: Matelda. What appears in the comparison is only cosa, a thing, and its verb is the verb of the event again: apparve, appare. Okey’s prose, the version Auden’s class had to write out from memory, keeps the order: appeared, then the comparison, then a lady solitary.
lenses.why: The subject is held back behind a comparison about a sudden sight that drives out other thoughts, so the sentence tells the wonder first and brings the lady only after it.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, in the Italian and in Okey’s prose. *Soletto* in the *Enciclopedia Dantesca*, under *solo*. The lady’s name: [Canto 33](#/read/dante-italian/pur-33:39), line 119. The examination: Donald Pearce’s memoir, pp. 153–54, which names this canto among those Auden announced.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: zeugma
lenses.plain: one verb is made to serve two clauses: it is said in the first and left out of the second
lenses.caption: Perdette, lost, is said once and serves two clauses: the mother lost the girl, and the girl lost the spring. With the verb in the line before, the last line holds two pairs: the mother and lei (her); ella (she) and the spring. The two words for the girl meet at the comma. On one side she is what is lost, on the other the one who loses. Okey’s prose says the verb twice. Primavera returns at the canto’s end: here, the lady says, it is always spring. In the myth Pluto, god of the underworld, carries Proserpina off. Chiavacci Leonardi’s commentary reads it as the loss of innocence, which Christians could take for the loss of this garden.
lenses.why: One verb is made to cover two losses, so the mother’s loss and the girl’s are told together, and the girl stands on both sides of the comma, as the one lost and the one who loses.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, in the Italian and in Okey’s prose. Zeugma, and the kind of it called prozeugma, as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines them. The lady’s words near the end of [the canto](#/read/dante-italian/pur-28:47). Anna Maria Chiavacci Leonardi’s commentary on line 49, at the Dartmouth Dante Project. The myth: Hermann Oelsner’s note on lines 49 to 51 in the Temple Classics edition; *Plutonian* in *A New English Dictionary*.

lenses.caption: The first sight of the lady is made partly of other poets’ words. In a song by Dante’s friend Guido Cavalcanti a shepherd girl goes sola sola, all alone, through a wood, singing. Dante’s lady is soletta, and commentators name the song at that line. The next canto opens by nearly repeating a line of the song. The second source Dante points to himself: she makes him rimembrar (remember) Proserpina, and primavera and the flowers are in Ovid’s telling, where the grove has perpetuum ver, lasting spring. At the canto’s end the lady says that the old poets who sang of the golden age perhaps dreamed of this place.
lenses.why: The lady comes in words that recall a friend’s love song and Ovid’s tale of Proserpina, and the canto ties the old poets to the garden: they sang of a golden age, she says, and perhaps dreamed of this place.
lenses.stands: Guido Cavalcanti’s song “In un boschetto trova’ pasturella,” lines 7 and 12, beside these lines and the first line of [Canto 29](#/read/dante-italian/pur-29:0); the commentaries of Charles S. Singleton and Anna Maria Chiavacci Leonardi name the song here. Dante’s *Vita nuova*, chapter III. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 5.385–401, and Hermann Oelsner’s note on lines 49 to 51. *Primavera* in the *Enciclopedia Dantesca*. The lady’s words near the end of [the canto](#/read/dante-italian/pur-28:46).

lenses.label: Measure
lenses.meterName: eleven syllables: the last accent always on the tenth and, as a rule, another on the fourth or the sixth

points.say: Two vowels meet between two words and count as one syllable. It happens four times in these nine lines.
The stress lands on the third syllable and the sixth, and the fourth is unstressed.
The two things she is doing take the same two places, third and sixth.
*Lei* on the fourth, *ella* on the sixth. At the comma the vowels of *lei* and *ed* meet and are kept apart.

lenses.caption: Dante’s line has eleven syllables, the last accent always on the tenth and, as a rule, another on the fourth or the sixth. Vowels that meet between words usually count as one syllable. The first three lines each open on five syllables stressed on the fourth: e là m’apparve, subitamente, per maraviglia. The two lines that bring the lady have no stress on the fourth: their main stress is on the sixth. Their first seven syllables hold the whole subject, una donna soletta, then two things she is doing, cantando, scegliendo. In the last line lei and ella take the fourth and sixth places, and the vowels that meet at the comma between them are kept apart.
lenses.why: The line changes kind where the held-back subject arrives, and its longer first half holds the subject whole; in the Proserpina line the two words for the girl take the fourth and sixth stresses, with a break between.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, counted by the rules of the Italian line. The rules: Claudio Ciociola’s article *endecasillabo* in the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano*, for the two kinds of line, whose first halves have five syllables and seven; the Treccani *Vocabolario* under *endecasillabo*, *sinalefe* and *dialefe*, for vowels that run together or stay apart.

grounds.claim: where the stresses fall, and where vowels run together or stay apart; the examiner counted the nine lines before reading these marks and agrees with them

the eleven-syllable line: a stress on the tenth and on the fourth or the sixth; the two kinds of line, whose first halves equal a five-syllable and a seven-syllable line; a line with no stress on the fourth is of the second kind, with a lighter stress on the second or third
grounds.source: Claudio Ciociola, endecasillabo, in Enciclopedia dell’Italiano (Treccani, 2010); Treccani, Vocabolario, endecasillabo

grounds.claim: vowels that meet between words count once, or are kept apart when the first is stressed
grounds.source: Treccani, Vocabolario, sinalefe and dialefe

auden.says: In the notes to *New Year Letter*, printed in 1941, the year of the course, Auden copied out two passages of the *Purgatorio* in the prose he would set his class. One is the nine lines of the second passage here, with the same six lines left out. The other is the three lines that close the first passage. Two lines from earlier in the same exchange stand in Italian at the head of a section of “Balaam and His Ass,” the essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* that sets Dante against *The Tempest*.
auden.source: *New Year Letter* (London: Faber, 1941), the note just before the note to line 1432 and the note to line 1705; “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 139
auden.checked: New Year Letter: seen by the examiner on 2026-10-03 in search snippets of the Faber edition at archive.org (newyearletter0000aude). One note quotes canto 17.91-96, a gap, then 103-105; the note headed Line 1705 quotes canto 15.73-75; both in Okey's wording, compared with dante-temple/pur-17, blocks 30, 31 and 34, and dante-temple/pur-15, block 24. Not seen in full. The Dyer's Hand read in the scan, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 6680-6698: p. 139 is the head of section IX of the essay, with two epigraphs, Luke 22:26 and canto 15, lines 55-56, in Italian.

auden.says: In the poem itself a poet may choose which of the dead masters will judge him, and when Auden’s name is called it is Dante who presides on his case. Dante, the lines say, wrecked a career in the world, brought all his powers of feeling, sense, will and mind to what lies beyond it, and had rational love, which Auden names in Latin, for his guide through the three realms of the dead.
auden.source: *New Year Letter* (1941), Part I, in *The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden* (1945), pp. 269–70
auden.checked: read by the examiner on 2026-10-03 in the open scan of The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden (New York: Random House, 1945) at archive.org: the lines begin at the foot of p. 269 and run on to p. 270. Dante is not named; he is the judge presiding on the poet's case

auden.says: In an essay on *The Merchant of Venice* Auden quoted the three lines that close the first passage, in the same prose, as an instance of something well known: love and understanding breed their like. He went straight on to money. Once money could breed money in a trading economy, he wrote, it amused poets to use usury, a base trade, as a figure for love, the noblest of human acts.
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer's Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 10934-10946, and again by the examiner on 2026-10-03; the scan drops the last word of the sentence that brings in the quotation, and a search snippet of the 1962 copy at archive.org (dyershandotheres0000aude) gives it: understanding

auden.says: In June 1941, near the end of a review of a book about romantic love, Auden quoted the words about the seed in Italian. Eros, he wrote, is that love: the basic will of every creature to become itself, and no creature can exist without it.
auden.quote: Agape is that Eros mutated by Grace, a conversion, not an addition, the Law fulfilled, not the Law destroyed
auden.source: “Eros and Agape,” a review of Denis de Rougemont, *Love in the Western World*, *The Nation*, 28 June 1941; in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 137–40
auden.checked: seen by the examiner on 2026-10-03 in search snippets of the scanned Prose, volume II, at archive.org (prosetravelbooks0000aude): the seed line in Italian, the sentence on Eros, and the words quoted here, which are exact. The review does not end on that sentence: it goes on after it and closes on another. The index gives p. 137 for the review. Not seen in full; not among the scans

auden.says: Setting three lines of the second passage against *The Tempest*, Auden added that no animal can fall. The tempter’s promise is in the future tense; a creature that only obeys necessity cannot picture doing what has never been done. The Italian he prints has too little before too much, the other way round from the Italian printed here.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 130–31
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer's Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 6266-6306

auden.says: By Donald Pearce’s account, the final examination was to write out cantos of the poem from memory, in the prose version that, Auden told the class, Eliot had used for *The Waste Land*. Pearce gives canto 28 as his one example of the *Purgatorio* cantos Auden announced. When the class protested, Auden cut seven cantos to five. Pearce wrote for three hours and filled five examination books.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 153–54
auden.checked: read in the scan of Pearce's essay, research/auden/pearce.txt: the announcement is on p. 153 and the examination on p. 154. In this scan each page number stands at the foot of its page, before the next page's heading.

auden.says: For Auden the master of dream literature is Dante. In him, he wrote, an endless flow of images goes together with a strict structure of logic and number that settles even how many verses there are.
auden.source: “George MacDonald,” the introduction to *The Visionary Novels of George MacDonald* (1954), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 269
auden.checked: read in the scan of Forewords and Afterwords, research/auden/fa.txt, lines 12838-12841; the scan drops punctuation

auden.says: Writing on Kierkegaard in 1952, Auden quoted the soul on the sixth terrace who says that he calls his suffering pain and ought to call it solace (canto 23, lines 70 to 72). The lines, he wrote, state the paradox of the place suffering has in Christianity: its message is in the end good news, and to a man’s self-love it is at first the worst of news.
auden.source: “Søren Kierkegaard,” the introduction to *The Living Thoughts of Kierkegaard* (1952), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 169
auden.checked: read in the scan of Forewords and Afterwords, research/auden/fa.txt, lines 8086-8099, and again by the examiner on 2026-10-03. caveats: Auden’s two notes in *New Year Letter* and his review of 1941 were read here only in extracts from scanned copies, not in full.

The examination is known from one student’s memoir, Donald Pearce’s. He names Canto 28 among the cantos Auden first announced, and does not say which five were kept. Other students remembered six cantos.

The verb *s’intende* in the first passage is read three ways: comprehend each other (Okey), aspire (Longfellow) and love (the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* and several commentators). Auden’s remark on love and understanding matches Okey’s wording.

In the second passage the Italian printed here has too much before too little. The Temple Classics edition, whose prose Auden set, prints its Italian with too little first, and so does Auden when he quotes the lines.

The second passage leaves out lines 97 to 102 of its canto, and the third leaves out lines 43 to 48. The stresses marked in the third are one reader’s count by the rules of Italian verse; in two of its lines a syllable could fairly be marked otherwise.
